🌲 - 🇱🇧 🇱🇧 LBCI reports that Hezbollah's security committee removed a mobile phone belonging to one of the five suspected Hezbollah operatives arrested in the Batroun–Bsharri highlands, preventing investigators from examining its contents. The phone had been left charging inside an apartment in Bnehran, Koura, while the other four detainees told investigators their devices were in Choueifat and Beirut's southern suburbs. LBCI attributed the removal to the premature disclosure of the arrests. Bilal al-Assaad, a Bnehran resident, was identified as the owner of the Honda CR-V used by the detainees. He was questioned and released pending investigation.

🌲 - 🇱🇧 ✝️ 🇱🇧 Allegations circulated by Al-Mahatta about masked Lebanese-speaking individuals accompanying Israeli troops at checkpoints in southern Lebanon have prompted warnings over accusations of collaboration targeting Christian border villages. According to Nidaa al-Watan, the villages of Rmeish, Ain Ebel, and Debel reject these unsubstantiated allegations, emphasizing that residents travel in convoys coordinated by municipalities and the Lebanese Army. The report warns that such accusations could endanger residents and threaten civil peace.

🌲 - ❗️ 🇱🇧 🇱🇧 Judge Claude Ghanem has filed charges against Hezbollah operatives Mohammad Rashid, Hussein Dbouk, Hassan Fneish, Mohammad Awada, and Qozhiya Allaw arrested in the Batroun–Bsharri highlands for offenses against Lebanon's internal state security.

🌲 - ‼️ 🇱🇧 🇱🇧 Investigators recovered three intact documents from the Batroun-Bcharri case detailing weapons allocations, military assignments, and coded names, alongside reconstructed fragments of torn papers. The arrests followed intelligence provided by foreign agencies rather than a chance encounter with police. Investigators are examining whether the group was preparing to use the mountainous area to launch long-range rockets. The evidence contributed to charging them all, with additional suspects facing prosecution.

🌲 - 🇱🇧 🇱🇧 Hezbollah is angered by the leaking of names of its operatives appearing in the Batroun–Bsharri and Dahr al-Baidar investigation files. A source close to Hezbollah accused members of Lebanon's judicial and security institutions of disclosing sensitive information to outside parties, warning that exposing the identities and roles of Hezbollah officials could make them targets of Israeli operations.

🌲 - 🇱🇧 🇱🇧 A senior Lebanese judicial source said that the five suspected Hezbollah operatives arrested in the Batroun–Bsharri highlands gave contradictory explanations during interrogation, initially claiming they were buying a car, then organizing food assistance, and later preparing for possible wartime displacement. Investigators recovered documents listing Kalashnikov rifles, RPG-7 rocket launchers, snipers, ambushes, and mines across northern Lebanon. The detainees' families told investigators that members of Hezbollah's security committee collected their mobile phones shortly after the arrests became public, preventing authorities from examining the devices. The five defendants are expected to appear before Military Investigating Judge Ghada Abou Alwan on November 19.

🌲 - 🇱🇧 🇱🇧 Lebanese security and judicial authorities have formally summoned Hezbollah's northern regional official, Sheikh Reda Ismail Ahmad, for questioning in connection with the five suspected Hezbollah operatives arrested in the Batroun–Bsharri highlands. His name emerged during preliminary interrogations and the examination of seized documents. Investigators also plan to summon additional Hezbollah officials and members whose names or aliases appeared in the evidence. Their statements will be added to the Military Court's case file as authorities seek to determine organizational and operational responsibilities.

🌲 - 🇱🇧 🇱🇧 Sources close to Hezbollah claim that an arrangement had been reached to release the five members detained in the Batroun–Bsharri highlands, but Lebanese authorities decided to abandon this arrangement and file criminal charges instead. Hezbollah views the prosecutions as part of a broader effort to pressure the organization through Lebanon's judicial institutions.
